name: R
year_note: Binary copies of R were placed on StatLib and announced on the s-news mailing list in August 1993
org: University of Auckland (Department of Statistics); now maintained by the R Core Team as a GNU project
runs: The R interpreter reads and evaluates source directly; most user-visible functions are themselves written in R, and they can call procedures written in C, C++ or Fortran.
what: R is a language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. It began as a free reimplementation of the S language from Bell Laboratories: it looks like S on the surface, while its implementation and semantics come from Scheme. Whole vectors and tables of data are the basic values, so a statistical analysis reads close to the mathematics.

name: Julia
year_note: Public announcement in the blog post "Why We Created Julia", 14 February 2012
typing: dynamic, with optional type annotations and type inference
runs: Julia code is compiled to machine code just in time, function by function, using type inference and the LLVM compiler framework.
what: Julia is a dynamic language for scientific and numerical computing. Scientists had largely moved to slower dynamic languages for daily work; Julia's authors wanted one language that is as easy to use as those and as fast as C. Its central idea is multiple dispatch, where the function body that runs is chosen by the types of all the arguments.

designers: Jack Little (rewrite in C, with Steve Bangert)
runs: MATLAB is a proprietary environment from MathWorks: commands and script files are executed interactively by the MATLAB program.
influenced_by: LINPACK and EISPACK (the libraries it was written to give access to)
what: MATLAB, short for Matrix Laboratory, is a programming and numeric computation environment for engineers and scientists. Cleve Moler wrote the first version in Fortran so that his students could use the LINPACK and EISPACK matrix libraries without writing Fortran programs; in that version the matrix was the only data type. It is a commercial product, unlike most languages on this map.

name: Lisp
year_note: John McCarthy's paper "Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine, Part I" appeared in Communications of the ACM in April 1960; implementation at MIT began in fall 1958
runs: Lisp expressions are read as lists and evaluated, by an interpreter or after compilation, usually inside an interactive session that keeps the running program open to change.
what: Lisp is a family of languages built on one idea: programs and data share a single form, the parenthesized list. McCarthy designed it for artificial intelligence work on symbolic expressions rather than numbers. Because code is data, a Lisp program can build and transform other programs, and garbage collection was devised for its first implementation. Common Lisp, Scheme and Emacs Lisp are among its living dialects.

notable.name: GNU Emacs

name: Haskell

designers: a committee formed at the FPCA '87 conference; the 1.0 report was edited by Paul Hudak and Philip Wadler, and later editors include Simon Peyton Jones and John Hughes

what: Haskell is a purely functional language: functions have no hidden side effects, values never change, and expressions are evaluated only when their results are needed. A committee created it in the late 1980s because more than a dozen similar lazy functional languages existed and researchers wanted one common, open standard. Its type system, especially type classes, has shaped many later languages.

name: OCaml
year_note: First release under the name Objective Caml in 1996; its ancestors Caml Light (1990) and Caml Special Light (1995) came earlier
runs: OCaml source is compiled either to bytecode for a small virtual machine or to native machine code by ocamlopt; a garbage collector manages memory.
what: OCaml is a functional language from the ML family that also allows imperative and object-oriented code. It grew out of a long line of research on ML at Inria, and it pairs a strong type system that infers types for you with a fast native compiler. That mix makes it a favorite for programs that manipulate other programs: compilers, type checkers, verifiers.

name: Erlang
year_note: Joe Armstrong began work on the language at the Ericsson Computer Science Laboratory in 1986; it was used inside Ericsson for years before being released as open source
runs: Erlang modules are compiled to bytecode that runs on the Erlang virtual machine, which schedules many lightweight processes and lets code be replaced while the system keeps running.
what: Erlang was created at Ericsson to program telephone switches: systems that handle huge numbers of simultaneous calls and are never supposed to stop. A program is a crowd of small isolated processes that share nothing and talk only by sending messages, so one can crash and be restarted without taking the rest down. The language started life as a modified Prolog, which is where its syntax comes from.

notable.name: Ericsson AXD301

It is a way to get the reliability of a telephone switch in a language that feels closer to Ruby.

name: Fortran

designers: John Backus and his team at IBM
runs: A Fortran compiler such as GFortran translates the source ahead of time into machine code.
what: Fortran, short for formula translation, is one of the earliest high-level languages and became the first computer language standard. Before it, programs were hand-coded as rows of zeros and ones; Backus wanted a language that captured the human intent of a program and left it to a compiler to recast that for the machine. It is still revised (the current standard is Fortran 2023) and still carries much of the world's numerical computing.

name: COBOL

what: COBOL, the common business-oriented language, was designed so that business data processing programs would read like English and run on computers from different makers. Its programs are organized around records with exactly declared fields, which suits payroll, accounts and ledgers. It is old and verbose, and a large amount of banking and government processing still depends on it.

name: SQL
year_note: Chamberlin and Boyce presented "SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language" at the ACM SIGFIDET workshop in May 1974; ANSI standardized SQL in 1986 and ISO in 1987
typing: static column types declared in a schema (strictness varies by database)
runs: A database engine parses the query, plans how to answer it, and executes that plan against stored tables; you state what rows you want, not how to find them.
what: SQL is the language for asking questions of relational databases, where data lives in tables. It was created at IBM, first under the name SEQUEL, to make Edgar Codd's relational model usable through English-like keywords. A query describes the result wanted and the database decides how to compute it, which is why the same query works on a phone and on a data warehouse.

name: Prolog
year_note: A preliminary version existed at the end of 1971 and a more definitive version, with the name Prolog, at the end of 1972 in Marseille
runs: A Prolog system loads facts and rules, then answers a query by searching for values that make it true, using unification and backtracking (SLD resolution).
what: Prolog is a logic programming language: a program is a set of facts and rules, and running it means asking a question that the system tries to prove. It came out of a project in Marseille to process natural language, and its name abbreviates the French for programming in logic. The same predicate can often be run in several directions, to check an answer or to search for one.

The early HTML was an SGML format, and CSS was added a few years later so that authors could style pages without bending the markup.

Since version 4 Lean is mostly written in Lean itself, and its large community library Mathlib has made it a main vehicle for formalizing modern mathematics.

year_note: Version 4.10, the first released system with an extensible set of tactics, came out in 1989; the first implementation of the Calculus of Constructions was started in 1984. The Coq Proof Assistant was renamed the Rocq Prover
typing: static, dependent types (Calculus of Inductive Constructions)
runs: The Rocq Prover checks definitions and proofs with a relatively small kernel, and can extract certified programs to OCaml, Haskell or Scheme.
what: Rocq, known as Coq until its recent renaming, is a proof assistant: a language for writing mathematical definitions, programs and proofs that the machine checks step by step. It is built on the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, in which a proof is a program and a theorem is its type. Programs proved correct in it can be extracted to run as ordinary OCaml or Haskell code.

Fixpoint gcd (a b : nat) : nat :=
  match a with
  | O => b
  | S a' => gcd (Nat.modulo b (S a')) (S a')
  end.

Compute gcd 48 18.

Example gcd_48_18 : gcd 48 18 = 6.
Proof. reflexivity. Qed.

name: Isabelle
year_note: Lawrence Paulson's paper "Natural Deduction as Higher-Order Resolution", which describes Isabelle as under development, appeared in the Journal of Logic Programming in 1986
org: University of Cambridge and Technische Universität München
typing: static (the types of higher-order logic, in Isabelle/HOL)
runs: Isabelle checks theory files interactively: every proof step is reduced to inferences of a small trusted core in the LCF tradition, and Isabelle/HOL can export executable definitions as SML, OCaml, Haskell or Scala code.
what: Isabelle is a generic proof assistant: a system in which mathematical statements are written in a formal language and proved with machine-checked steps. Its most used form, Isabelle/HOL, works in higher-order logic and offers strong automation plus a proof language meant to be read by people. It follows the LCF approach, where only a small core can create theorems, so extensions cannot break soundness.

notable.name: Archive of Formal Proofs

name: TLA+
year_note: Lamport's "Specifying Concurrent Systems with TLA+" was published in 1999
runs: A TLA+ specification is not executed: the TLC model checker explores every reachable state of a small instance to look for violations, and the TLAPS proof system checks hand-written proofs.
what: TLA+ is a language for describing what a system should do before, or beside, writing its code. A specification is plain mathematics: a formula for the possible starting states and a formula for the allowed steps. It was made for concurrent and distributed systems, where bugs come from rare interleavings of events that testing misses but an exhaustive model checker finds.

notable.name: Amazon Web Services
notable.text: AWS has used TLA+ since 2011 and its engineers published an article in April 2015 on how it is used on their systems.

notable.name: Azure Cosmos DB
notable.text: Microsoft's Cosmos DB team used TLA+ to specify and validate the core algorithms and the consistency levels of its globally distributed database.

sample.code:
---- MODULE TheAlgorithmInTLA ----
EXTENDS Integers
CONSTANTS M, N
VARIABLES x, y
Init == (x = M) /\ (y = N)
Next == \/ /\ x < y
           /\ y' = y - x
           /\ x' = x
        \/ /\ y < x
           /\ x' = x - y
           /\ y' = y
====
sample.how: Not run: no TLA+ tools on this Mac. This is Figure 2 of Leslie Lamport's paper "Euclid Writes an Algorithm: A Fairytale" (https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/euclid.pdf), typed in ASCII (12 lines, kept whole). It describes the subtraction form of Euclid's algorithm as an initial condition and a next-state relation; with M = 48 and N = 18 every behavior stops at x = y = 6.

name: Dafny

runs: The Dafny verifier translates the program and its specifications to the Boogie intermediate language and asks the Z3 solver to prove them; verified code is then compiled to C#, Java, JavaScript, Go or Python.
what: Dafny is a programming language with verification built in. Next to ordinary code you write what each method requires and guarantees, and a static verifier tries to prove, automatically and while you type, that the code meets those promises. It aims to make proving a program correct feel like getting it to compile.

notable.name: AWS Encryption SDK for Dafny
notable.text: Amazon publishes an implementation of its client-side encryption library, the AWS Encryption SDK, in Dafny.

name: Solidity
year_note: Solidity was publicly previewed for the first time in November 2014 at Devcon0; version numbering in the codebase began in July 2015
designers: the Solidity team of the Ethereum project
runs: The solc compiler turns Solidity into bytecode for the Ethereum Virtual Machine; the bytecode is stored on the blockchain and executed by every node of the network when the contract is called.
what: Solidity is a statically typed, curly-bracket language for writing smart contracts: programs that live on the Ethereum blockchain and control accounts and assets there. Once deployed, a contract runs inside a peer-to-peer network where nobody has special authority over its execution.
